subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: pairing the news with a recovery plan [Action]
passage: Pema, you want to know how to give a client bad news? Let me tell you about a time I did it well enough. I'm Reena. I was a young woman of twenty-six, so nervous my tea went cold. The migration had failed and the go-live would slip. I named the cause plainly, once. I said sorry once, not five times. Then I put a page on the screen: week one, week two, week three, each with a name beside it, and a promise of a short update every Tuesday and Friday. The client's operations head stopped asking how this could have happened and started asking about week two. They could judge the recovery, not just the problem. That was the whole trick, if you can call it one.

qa.q: On which days did Reena promise updates?
qa.a: Reena promised a short update every Tuesday and Friday.

qa.q: How was Reena feeling before giving the news?
qa.a: Reena was so nervous that the tea went cold.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped the client stay engaged, and why?
qa.a: Putting up a page with weeks and named owners helped, because the client could judge the recovery instead of only dwelling on the problem.

qa.q: How did the client's operations head see the plan?
qa.a: The operations head probably felt steadier, since the plan gave something concrete to ask about and shifted the questions from blame to week two.

grounding: Illustrates giving the cause, one apology and a weekly plan with named owners and regular updates so a client can judge the recovery.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
passage: In a small-town branch of a cooperative bank, Harish sat across from the manager, Omkar, with his laptop half open. "The delay wasn't us," Harish began. "The infrastructure team took the servers down twice and gave us no notice." Omkar's eyebrows went up. "So who at your company answers for that?" Harish shifted in the plastic chair. "That's their side." "I'm not dealing with their side," Omkar said. "I'm dealing with you." Outside, a bus horn blared. Harish had brought a new date but never reached that slide. Omkar asked to hear from a senior person at the vendor before the next meeting, and wrote two names in his notebook: Harish's, and the vendor's director.

qa.q: Whom did Harish say was responsible for the delay?
qa.a: Harish said the infrastructure team took the servers down twice and gave no notice.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling on hearing "That's their side"?
qa.a: Omkar was irritated and doubtful, feeling that nobody on the vendor's side was taking responsibility.

qa.q: What could Harish have done instead of blaming another team, and why?
qa.a: Harish could have owned the problem on behalf of the company, explained what would change and given the new date, because a client wants someone accountable and a plan.

qa.q: How might the infrastructure team feel if they heard how Harish described the delay?
qa.a: They might feel unfairly singled out and less willing to help, which shows how blaming weakens confidence in both teams.

grounding: Illustrates a messenger blaming another team for a problem so the client hears excuses and asks who is accountable on the vendor side.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: reviewing the call and adjusting communication cadence [Revision]
passage: Review note after the client call, written by Deepika, delivery manager. I sat in on Chaitanya's call with the client on Tuesday. The client was not angry about the delay itself. They said twice that they had found out late and wanted to hear from us more often. Afterwards Chaitanya and I sat with the team and went through the notes. A weekly email was clearly not enough. We changed it: a short note every Monday and Thursday, three lines each: done, next, worries. Chaitanya wrote the first one that afternoon. A week later the client replied, "This is what I needed," and stopped phoning the account manager directly. I will keep watching for three weeks to check it is not turning into a chore.

qa.q: On which days do the short notes go out?
qa.a: The short notes go out every Monday and Thursday.

qa.q: What was the client feeling about the way they were kept informed?
qa.a: The client felt left in the dark and worried, having found out late and wanting to hear more often.

qa.q: What else could the team do to keep the notes useful, and why?
qa.a: The team could ask the client after a month whether three lines are enough, because the right rhythm may change as the project moves.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt after the client's reply?
qa.a: Chaitanya probably felt relieved and encouraged, since a small change in habit had steadied the relationship.

grounding: Illustrates reviewing a client call, finding the client wanted more frequent updates and switching to short Monday and Thursday notes.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: delegating the message to the person with the relationship [Thinking]
passage: An hour before the call with Noor, Seema had her slides ready: the cause, the new date, the recovery steps. Then she remembered the last three meetings. Noor had put every question to Rajiv, the delivery head, and given Seema only a polite nod. "The message is fine," Seema thought. "The messenger isn't the person Noor trusts. That isn't about my ego. It's about whether Noor stays open to the plan." She rang Rajiv, who was stuck in a taxi. "Can you join and lead, and I'll cover the details?" "I'll be there in twenty minutes," he said. On the call Rajiv gave the news in two sentences. Noor listened, then asked, "And what's the plan?" Seema shared her slides.

qa.q: How long before the call was Seema's preparation ready?
qa.a: Seema had her slides ready an hour before the call.

qa.q: What did Seema realise while thinking about the last three meetings?
qa.a: Seema realised Noor trusted Rajiv most and might stay open to the news only if he led, and she put her ego aside.

qa.q: What else could Seema do to help Rajiv lead well, and why?
qa.a: Seema could send Rajiv the key points and the recovery steps before he joins, because the person leading needs the facts to hand.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Rajiv opens the call?
qa.a: Noor probably feels reassured to hear the news from someone trusted, which makes it easier to listen to the recovery plan.

grounding: Illustrates an account lead realising the client trusts the delivery head most and asking him to join and lead so the client stays open to the recovery plan.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: listening separately to each side first [Action]
passage:
Thursday. Sat with Minakshi first, half an hour in the small meeting room, and asked only two questions: what happened, and what do you need? Minakshi said Tarun kept rewriting the release script without telling anyone. Then Tarun, who said Minakshi had blocked his changes "for no reason" and that he just wanted to know what he owns. I said nothing about who was right. What I noticed: both described the same gap in different words. Nobody had ever said who owns the release task. Both of them looked relieved just to have been listened to. Tomorrow I'll draw up an ownership list and show it to each of them separately before we all meet.

Devika

qa.q: What two questions did Devika ask each colleague?
qa.a: Devika asked what happened and what do you need.

qa.q: How did Minakshi and Tarun seem to feel after being listened to?
qa.a: Both looked relieved, since each had been able to tell their side without being judged.

qa.q: What could Devika do next, and why?
qa.a: Devika could draft an ownership list and show it to each of them before they meet, because a clear owner for each task removes the gap the quarrel grew from.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt about the release script being blocked?
qa.a: Tarun probably felt frustrated and unsure of the role, wanting to know what Tarun owns.

grounding: Illustrates a lead meeting two colleagues one at a time, asking what happened and what each needs, and finding the quarrel began over unclear ownership of a release task.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
passage: I'm Samir, and I was in the room when Simran sat down with Anil and Tanya after their third argument that month. Simran did not ask who was to blame. "Why did the deploy fail?" "Because the config was old." "Why was it old?" "Because I thought Tanya updated it," Anil said. "Why did you think that?" "Because we both had that ticket." "And why did you both have it?" Silence. Then Anil said, "Nobody wrote down who owns it." Simran wrote two lines on the whiteboard: overlap, and no handover note. The tension in the room dropped. I can't say if Simran planned to ask so many times. It just kept going until it stopped being about personalities.

qa.q: What two things did Simran write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Simran wrote overlap, and no handover note.

qa.q: What might Anil have been feeling when saying nobody wrote down who owns it?
qa.a: Anil probably felt a mix of relief and some embarrassment at seeing that the problem was not personal.

qa.q: What else could Simran do once the cause was found, and why?
qa.a: Simran could set a single owner per ticket and a handover note, because that removes the overlap that kept creating blame.

qa.q: How might Tanya have felt when the questions stayed off blame?
qa.a: Tanya probably felt relieved and less defensive, seeing that the trouble came from how the work was assigned.

grounding: Illustrates a lead asking why repeatedly and finding overlapping assignments and a missing handover note behind the quarrel, not personalities.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: clarifying roles and shared working rules [Action]
passage:
Simran: I've drafted a list. Chetan, you own the release script. Nidhi, you own testing and the handover note.
Chetan: So if the script breaks, it's mine.
Simran: Yes. And if the handover note is missing, that's Nidhi's.
Nidhi: What should the note look like?
Simran: Three lines: what changed, what's left, who to ask. Same format every time.
Chetan: I can live with that.
Nidhi: Same. Can we put it in the team doc?
Simran: It's already there. Please both reply "confirmed" under it.
Chetan: Confirmed.
Nidhi: Confirmed.
Simran: Good. Next time we start arguing over whose job something was, we open the list instead of the old fight.

qa.q: What three lines does the handover note contain?
qa.a: The note has three lines: what changed, what's left, who to ask.

qa.q: What might Chetan be feeling when asking whether the broken script is Chetan's?
qa.a: Chetan is probably wary about blame, checking what is being asked before agreeing.

qa.q: What else could Simran do so the rules keep working, and why?
qa.a: Simran could review the list with both after a couple of weeks, because roles may need small changes once the work shifts.

qa.q: How might Nidhi see the list?
qa.a: Nidhi probably sees it as fair, since each job has a clear owner and there is one format for the note.

grounding: Illustrates a lead writing a responsibility list, agreeing a handover format and asking both colleagues to confirm, so a rule replaces argument.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: facilitated joint conversation with agreed ground rules [Action]
passage:
Monday. Brought Mahima and Sahil together in the small room at four, with three rules on a card: one person speaks at a time, talk about the work and not the person, finish by each asking for a single change. I was nervous. Mahima said her piece, and Sahil did not interrupt, though his jaw tightened. Then Sahil said his. When it came to requests, Mahima asked to be told before her tickets are moved, and Sahil asked for comments on his code within a day. Two changes, on trial for a fortnight. I'll check in on the twenty-second. We ended with tea. They are not friends yet, but they walked out still talking about the release.

Pooja

qa.q: What were the two requests made at the end?
qa.a: Mahima asked to be told before her tickets are moved, and Sahil asked for comments on his code within a day.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel before the meeting?
qa.a: Pooja felt nervous.

qa.q: What could Pooja do on the twenty-second, and why?
qa.a: Pooja could ask each of them separately how the two changes are working, because people often say more one-to-one than in front of each other.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt while Mahima spoke first?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt tense, holding back an urge to interrupt, which his tightening jaw suggests.

grounding: Illustrates a lead bringing two colleagues together with ground rules and ending with one request each, leaving with two changes to try.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: hoping it fades without intervention [Pitfall]
passage:
Day 3. In the Monday meeting, Suraj said, "Some of us actually read the spec." Everyone heard it. Pradeep studied his notes and, wanting to avoid awkwardness, moved on to the next item.

Day 17. The comments in meetings got sharper. Two developers now ate lunch with Suraj, while the other three sat at the far table.

Day 34. Farhan, the target of most of the remarks, had a calendar entry marked "personal" on Wednesday afternoon. Pradeep guessed it was an interview. He asked in the last meeting, "Is everything okay with the team?" Nobody answered.

qa.q: What did Suraj say in the Monday meeting?
qa.a: Suraj said, "Some of us actually read the spec."

qa.q: Why did Pradeep move on to the next item?
qa.a: Pradeep wanted to avoid awkwardness, so he ignored the sharp comment and hoped the tension would fade.

qa.q: What could Pradeep have done on Day 3, and why?
qa.a: Pradeep could have spoken to Suraj privately that day about the remark, because a small talk early is easier than a divided team later.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt as the remarks continued?
qa.a: Farhan probably felt targeted and unsupported, which may be why Farhan started looking for another job.

grounding: Illustrates a lead ignoring sharp comments to avoid awkwardness, so tension spreads, others pick sides and one member starts looking for another job.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members
subtype: Approach: taking sides with the senior performer [Pitfall]
passage:
Wednesday. The row between Shankar and Ira over who owns the release checks came to me today. Shankar is the senior person, six years here and the best numbers on the team. I asked Ira to adjust. "Shankar has been here six years," I said, "so let's not change how he does it." Ira nodded and didn't argue. That was the first thing that bothered me. In the afternoon meeting Ira said nothing, and asked no question all day. The release checks still show two names on the board. Nobody has decided who owns them. I told myself I'd settled it. It doesn't feel settled.

Suraj

qa.q: How long has Shankar been at the firm?
qa.a: Shankar has been there six years.

qa.q: How did Ira probably feel after being asked to adjust?
qa.a: Ira probably felt dismissed and discouraged, which fits the silence for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What could Suraj do now, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could talk with Ira and Shankar about who owns the release checks and write it down, because the real gap is still open.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Suraj's decision?
qa.a: Shankar may feel backed up and relieved, and may not notice that the real question about ownership was never answered.

grounding: Illustrates a lead trusting the senior colleague and asking the junior one to adjust, leaving the junior quiet and the ownership gap unresolved.
